In brief

Thoughts of how the Huguenots brought their textile manufacturing to Ireland after fleeing persecution in France make Bloom recall a solo and chorus from the opera Les Huguenots, by Giacomo Meyerbeer: "La causa è santa! Tara tara. Great chorus that." The sacred cause is Catholics massacring Protestants, and it seems quite possible that another phrase that floats through Bloom's mind earlier in Lestrygonians, "God wants blood victim," was inspired by the same opera.

At more length

Set in Paris at the time of the late 16th century religious wars, Les Huguenots culminates in the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre of 1572.  With its lavish sets, exceptionally large and varied orchestra, strenuous virtuoso singing, and historical subject matter, the work helped to define the new genre of Grand Opera. It was tremendously popular in the 19th century: in the seventy years after its 1836 premiere, the Paris Opera performed the work more than 1,000 times, and many other opera houses around the world (London, Munich, New Orleans, Vienna, New York) staged productions. Dublin's Theatre Royal performed it in August 1859 and again in September and October 1904. Although the libretto by Eugène Scribe and Émile Deschamps is in French, opera houses in English-speaking countries often performed the work in Italian—the language of Bloom's recollection.

The opera's most gripping scene comes when the Comte de Saint Bris, a fanatical leader of the Catholic forces, leads a bénédiction des poignards (benediction of the daggers), making his fellow conspirators swear a solemn oath to exterminate the Huguenots. He sings the words "La causa è santa" (or "Pour cette cause sainte") to a rousing melody and the others take it up in the "chorus" that Bloom remembers. In act 5, in a suitably operatic climax, St. Bris orders his troops to fire on a Protestant crowd and the musket balls take the life of his own daughter.

After recalling the words about a sacred cause, Bloom does not think of the Huguenots, or religious strife, or the massacre of thousands of men, women, and children. Fixated on the lustrous fabrics in the Grafton Street shop windows, he thinks of washing clothes in rainwater and of "Pincushions. I'm a long time threatening to buy one." But there is good reason to suppose that the opera's subject matter is playing in his mind, and has been for some time. He recalls the chorus just after seeing "a flood of bloodhued poplin: lustrous blood. The huguenots brought that here"—and at the beginning of Lestrygonians he accepts a religious handout mentioning the "Blood of the Lamb" and thinks, "All are washed in the blood of the lamb. God wants blood victim. Birth, hymen, martyr, war, foundation of a building, sacrifice, kidney burntoffering, druids' altars."

As far as I know no critic has made the connecion, but The Huguenots ends with a chorus of soldiers singing, "Sian tutti messi a fil di spada; / Alfin lo stuol degli empi cada; / Feriam, struggiam,—è Dio ch 'l vuol" ("Let them all be put to the edge of the sword; / Finally, let the crowd of the wicked fall; / Let's strike, let's destroy,—it's God who wills it"). God wants blood victims, and in an entirely characteristic feat of associative genius Joyce interweaves that subversive theological view with believers washed in the blood of the Lamb, poplin washed in rainwater, Huguenot poplin the color of blood, and Huguenot blood washing the streets of Paris.

This reading of Lestrygonians becomes impossible if one accepts the Gabler edition's alteration of "La causa è santa. Tara tara" to "Lacaus esant tara tara." This is the form that the phrase takes in Nausicaa (there with no space between the nonsense words) as part of Bloom's seaside reveries. The mangling of the Italian in that chapter is arguably the result of a very sleepy man recalling the sound of the syllables rather than thinking of their semantic sense. Putting the mangled version in a more wakeful setting suggests that Bloom is simply ignorant of the meaning of the Italian phrase—which is possible given his general ignorance of Italian, but also unlikely given his familiarity with many Italian words and Italian operas. Joyce makes fun of Bloom's poor Italian more than once, starting in Calypso when he misremembers Mozart's Vorrei e non vorrei as Voglio e non vorrei. But this mistake is nothing so egregious as Lacaus esant, and Bloom corrects it two chapters later: "voglio e non vorrei. No: vorrei e non." 

In choosing "Lacaus esant," Gabler follows the text of the eighth chapter published in The Little Review in January 1919, preferring it to the 1922 first edition of Ulysses and all subsequent ones. The Rosenbach manuscript, which Joyce wrote out as he completed each chapter, makes no mention of Meyerbeer's opera as Bloom contemplates Huguenot textiles, and neither it nor The Little Review contains the two sentences that follow "All are washed in the blood of the lamb": "God wants blood victim. Birth, hymen, martyr, war, foundation of a building, sacrifice, kidney burnoffering, druids' altars." It seems likely that when Joyce wrote the earliest versions of Lestrygonians he did not know exactly what he wanted to do with Meyerbeer—and that, by the time of the Shakespeare and Company printing, he had decided to make the Italian correct and to amplify its meaning with a second passage suggesting the many ways in which human beings have propitiated their gods with blood sacrifice.

John Hunt 2026
